utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could make yourself comfortable. Before you begin, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Sir, I have some words for you. We are very glad to have you here to testify in these proceedings today, and I would like to advise you that the Chamber is aware of some of the concerns and difficulties you have raised concerning your testimony. However, I would like to advise you, firstly, that you have been granted protective measures, which continue to be in effect in these proceedings, and that your identity as a witness before the Tribunal will not be known to the public. Should you feel, at any time either during or after your testimony, that your protective measures have been compromised, you should inform us, through the Victims and Witnesses Section. Secondly, the Tribunal endeavours to ensure that your testimony is given with the least possible stress to yourself, and the Victims and Witnesses Section is ready to assist you should you have any problems in that regard while you are here. However, as you are aware, these are serious criminal proceedings, and both the Prosecution and the accused, Mr. Karadzic, have the right to ask you questions, which you should answer to the best of your ability and as concisely as possible. We hope to be able to finish your testimony today, but it is possible that we will need to complete it tomorrow afternoon. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. During your testimony, you will be referred to as Witness KDZ310, and nobody will use your name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 90143 displayed, but not broadcast, just displayed on the screens here in the courtroom, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at this page, is that your name on this page and also your birth -- date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the signatures at the bottom, is there your signature at the bottom and also the date of the amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we move into private session just for a very brief moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The information you provided in the statement and the testimony that we just mentioned were amalgamated in a statement, and we just saw the first page of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to review this statement and sign it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at it yesterday and changed some words, made some corrections, and then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you affirm that the amalgamated statement accurately reflects the information you provided in the past?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, would you provide the same information to the Court if questioned on these same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender Exhibit -- 65 ter 90143 for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P1937, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will provide a redacted public version shortly, because this document needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be given Exhibit P1938.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the Court's permission, I would now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence, as admitted. During the relevant period, the witness lived in Sarajevo and was a soldier in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The witness became aware that, as the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from Slovenia and parts of Croatia, huge quantities of weapons and ammunition were transported to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that as early as September 1991, weapons were delivered to Serbian Democratic Party members at JNA barracks. He observed that the JNA had established artillery positions around Sarajevo by 6th of April, 1992. The witness recalled the political tension in Sarajevo before the conflict. According to his observations, speeches of politicians, including the accused, and anti-Muslim and anti-Croat propaganda had an effect on the ordinary people and caused hatred against non-Serbs. Non-Serbs were described as a threat to the Serbs and other ethnic -- and that ethnic divisions would be necessary. The witness observed that Serbs took control over Grbavica in mid-May 1992 without any resistance and that non-Serbs were subjected to restrictive and repressive measures, abuse and crimes. They were expelled, and their departments [sic] looted. According to the witness's observations, the military chain of command and the communication within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps functioned. The witness observed the deployment of soldiers with sniper assignments in various positions in Grbavica. These soldiers used specific equipment. The witness became aware that they targeted civilians. The witness observed the shelling of the city from artillery and mortar positions and that the shelling often targeted civilian areas in a non-selective way. According to the witness, detainees from KPD Kula were forced to dig trenches on front-lines. Some of these detainees were killed while doing so. Your Honour, that concludes the summary, and I would now have a few additional questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, and I refer here to the paragraphs 3 to 6, you describe the tension between the various groups in -- ethnic groups in 1991 and 1992. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now like to have Exhibit -- 65 ter 11928 brought up on the screen, and this can be broadcast. And as it is coming up: It is a report from "Javnost" with the title "Memorial for the Souls of Innocents" of the 26th of January, 1991, about a ceremony held in the village of Vrhpraca, at the base of the Jahorina mountain, remembering the killing of Serbs and the deportation of others to Jasenovac during World War II. And if we can zoom in on the B/C/S, on the text, below the first picture. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you have an opportunity to study this document before coming into the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. I take it this witness was given the voice distortion as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is important to turn off the microphone when he's due to speak, so in order to avoid the overlap. So please make sure, before -- it's difficult. I'll make sure, but on your part, as well, please confirm that the other's microphone is off, the red light is -- when the red light is gone, and then you may speak. Do you understand, Mr. Witness. The red light of other speakers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where the red light is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The red lights you can see here burning on the speaker's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this kind of -- this particular ceremony, did you know about this particular ceremony or about similar ceremonies at that time? And we are talking here now about 1991.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we just go to the second page in the English. The B/C/S can remain as it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we see here that Mr. Karadzic is also giving a speech and speaks about the Serbs as the only people in the world who were persecuted and killed only because they exist, and "that is why we will no longer allow them to separate us and divide us in three states and gradually destroy us." Witness, what Mr. Karadzic is saying here, have you heard him speak in such terms at occasions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did these ceremonies and what was said here, did it have an effect on the people that you had communication with?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, it did have an effect on inter-ethnic relations, and, if necessary, I can explain what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The witness isn't in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am not getting in my ears the Serbian of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we try it again? Could you answer your last question, kindly, again, Mr. Witness? Shall we repeat the last question and answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did -- these kind of events and what was said, did it have an effect on inter-ethnic relations? And if so, can you explain in what way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, it did have an effect. And if needed, I can explain that, what kind of effect that it had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I noticed Mr. Karadzic saying to the effect that he does not get the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I hear only translation, but I have here the witness just physically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a quick adjournment in order to look into the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you say, "Good morning"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, do you hear me now? If I may begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you think we have to repeat the last question and answer? No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, would you -- would you just explain, in more details, what effect it had?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: It is stated there that only the Serbian people are the people who were killed, persecuted, and tortured in World War II. But in truth, all the three peoples suffered casualties, and all three peoples were victimised, they were persecuted and tortured. I cannot really give you any figures here. Specifically, in this text, the number of casualties is given, and the way it is stated, it incites inter-ethnic hatred, stating that only there are members of the Serbian ethnic group, and they determined the number of victims. There is an example. For example, Mr. Josipovic, the current president of Croatia, and the current president of Serbia, Mr. Tadic, went to Vukovar. The victims there -- actually, they honoured the victims in quite a different way, a way that can pave the way for reconciliation between the two peoples. An apology was given for the casualties. It wasn't just the Croats that were present to mark that occasion. In this case, there were Serbs who were speaking about Serbian victims, and this is something that incites ethnic hatred and does not make living together, a common life, possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is this "Javnost" a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a daily newspaper, "Borba," or some other Belgrade daily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the top left of this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it says "Javnost." That is some kind of daily newspaper, "Javnost," but I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1939, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now have the Exhibit -- 65 ter 01009 on the screen, and it can also be broadcast. And as it is coming up: It is an interview with Mr. Karadzic from "Nasa Borba" of the 16th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up: Sir, do you know the publication "Nasa Borba," and is it a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a daily newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we also have the English? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We see here it's an interview of 16 March 1992. Did you -- 1992, yes. And as it is coming up: Did you have an opportunity to study this document when you came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I had the opportunity yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we move the B/C/S version a bit so that we can see the beginning -- the beginning of this article. The English is okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If we look at the beginning, Mr. Karadzic says here that: "... the Serbs will never find peace until they have achieved their age-old aspiration of living in one state." Witness, are you aware of this aspiration of Serbs living in one state?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you hear Mr. Karadzic say things to this effect?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did this have an impact on the inter-ethnic relationship among the people that lived around you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, you know, at the time Mr. Karadzic was a charismatic person, a charismatic figure among the Serbian people, and people trusted him, and he thought that it was an idea that was achievable.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have the second page in the English, while the B/C/S version is actually correct as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, Mr. Karadzic speaks about a trend of disorder and chaos that could lead to inter-ethnic and inter-religious war, with hundreds of thousands of dead and hundreds of towns destroyed. Witness, did you hear Mr. Karadzic make such statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you give an example? Do you recall anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: In many TV interviews, but also at the well-known Assembly session, Mr. Karadzic explained what could happen in case there were a war. That is what the general public knows. There was a statement made by him that it may happen that a particular people may disappear. It was the problem between the Serbs and Muslims, they were quite mixed, not the Serbs and Croats, so in that situation one people could disappear. That was a serious threat to peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to which people was he referring when speaking of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now have the third page in the English. The other one, the B/C/S, is still okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the top, Mr. Karadzic refers to maps and that more than half of all the territory belongs to Serbs, even where they are not in the majority population. And then he goes on further to more population figures and details. Were you aware that maps were being discussed at that time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall that there were also maps in relation to Sarajevo, and do you recall what was indicated in such maps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that maps of Sarajevo looked very similar to what the ultimate division according to the Dayton Agreement was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these maps and the divisions of territories, did these maps and the talks about it have an effect on the population?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: They did have an effect on the population, of course they did, especially the population that saw itself outside the areas that would belong to a particular people, say Serbs, who saw themselves outside a possible Serb area, according to such maps. Well, there was a feeling of anxiety among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the other ethnic groups; what was about -- what about their -- the effect on them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Of course, this had a negative effect on Croats and Muslims, who saw themselves living in the territory of another people or another nation, or, say, Muslims in a Serb territory, or Croats in a Serb territory. This made people feel unsafe, insecure and uncertain in terms of what might happen. At that time, a lot of people were saying that there might be a war, but what kind of war it would be, well, people were quite simply afraid. They were afraid for their families, they were afraid in terms of their very existence and their survival in that area. You know, that is a terrible thing. Croats and Muslims were afraid, and Serbs were afraid too, of course. Everybody was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now move to the seventh page in the English. And in relation to the text in B/C/S, we would need to have the second page and the end of the second page. I think it has to be -- I'm not sure, but it should be the end of the interview, not -- I think that's what you're showing. It should be -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, Mr. Karadzic refers to the fact that there are not many unsolved issues with the Croats, but that the Serbs and the Muslims cannot live together, but only beside each other. Did you hear him say words to this effect?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: His overall policy, as the top man of the SDS, led in that direction; namely, to prove to both peoples that they can no longer live together. However, he is not competent at all to decide who is going to live with who and who is going to be married, say, to a Croat woman, a Muslim woman, et cetera, to split up families, to spoil good relations, inter-human relations, as it were. However, in that case, an effort had to be made in order to lead to a situation that would ultimately result in war. People lived together for years, and we could have gone on living together. He and other politicians, like Izetbegovic and Kljujic, and no one, not God Almighty, is competent to decide who is going to live with who. Their intellectual and other activities were supposed to take place in a different area; improving the standard of living. We could have competed in the arts, in literature, in sports, not in terms of who could kill more members of another ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1940, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you described the take-over of Grbavica in mid-May 1992, and you spoke about the abuse of non-Serbs and the fear that it caused. And I refer here to the paragraphs 14 as well as 18 to 21. Can you give us the time-frame when this abuse and the expulsion of non-Serbs happened in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: This happened immediately when the soldiers came; I mean, when they came to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did it stop at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you refer to soldiers, after the soldiers came, does that mean -- who did the expulsion of non-Serbs; the soldiers, or police, or just others?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Both soldiers and the civilian and military police took part in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this concludes the examination-in-chief, and I would now request that the associated exhibits referred to in the amalgamated statement be admitted into evidence. Some of them need to be under seal, and I can state it as follows: Items 20266 need to be under seal. It's a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that all the exhibits, except for the item numbered as 40292B, are under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good. Thank you. Then I don't need to go through all of them. We will produce -- we will produce redacted versions of the photos and the maps, because all that needs to be done is to redact the signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the redacted version for the photocopy of --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it in the hands of the Court Deputy to consult with you, what public versions --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- will be produced in each item.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's mostly -- it's basically the photos and the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections from the Defence? So all of them will be admitted and given numbers by the Court Deputy and circulated to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Before you begin, I forgot to mention at the outset that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her personal urgent matters. And today we'll sit until 2.30, if necessary, with two half-hour breaks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all. I hope that we haven't forgotten each other over these past three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wish to tell you, at the very outset, that this Defence respects all the participants involved and all witnesses, so you really have no reason for concern or anxiety. We never attack witnesses. We only try to shed more light, with the assistance of witnesses, in terms of what they know, what they saw, what their immediate knowledge is, and what they learned through the media. So please let us focus on what your direct knowledge is. The learned Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff put quite a few political questions to you, quite a few political questions to you, so I would like to ask you where you got all that knowledge. Were you a member of a party, or some other particular team, or did you have some other sources of information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of any party, national or other, never in my life. Information, I got from my very own life. I lived in the area. I tried to obtain information impartially by establishing my own views on the basis of Belgrade's, Sarajevo's, Zagreb's, and other media, and talking to different people, Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, there's a further complication. In addition to waiting for his light being turned off, could you put a pause between the question and the answer, because your answer is to be translated by the interpreters. So could you wait -- could you put a pause, during which time the question can be fully translated. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand. However, I do not see the light on Mr. Karadzic's microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One tip I can give to you is that you may take a look at the transcript. When the transcript stops, that means the translation is over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have insight into some confidential materials or documents of any one of the parties involved or any state organs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, no. I am an ordinary person. I was not involved in politics at all. I did not work in any state institutions, I was not in any state organs. I was an ordinary citizen in that city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. See, I'm making -- I'm making a pause, too, just so you know. So you observed the political situation -- or, rather, you did not observe the political situation from the point of view of an expert. You did not really want to make an analysis. You simply gained impressions on the basis of the media. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You're right, in part. As I've already said, I did not gain impressions and knowledge only from the media. I gained impressions and knowledge from conversations with people, as I've already said. Some of these people knew more about politics and were more involved in that. I was not involved in politics then, and I'm not involved in politics now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, I think what is going to be far more important for these proceedings is what you directly saw, and that is what I am going to focus on during your examination. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, before we move on to those questions and some general questions, may I ask you whether you remember that in the Communist period, it was forbidden to perform religious rites at sites where people were victims of political persecution during the war on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There was no prohibition, specifically. However, it was not in that sense that these victims were being commemorated. Perhaps you're right, from that point of view. However, it was not only Serbs who were not allowed to do that, but all the peoples involved, all three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that all three peoples did have victims? However, do you agree that during the Second World War, Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: A larger part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that all of it was in the independent Republic of Croatia. You are right when you say that all three peoples suffered. However, do you agree that it was only the independent state of Croatia that had a racist legislation that legalised the killing of Serbs, Jews and Roma, and that no other state anywhere in Europe had that, except for Germany and Croatia? They had laws that permitted racist killings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you, for example, that Ante Pavelic and Milan Nedic regularly paid pensions to all citizens in the territory under their control, whereas in your state, Muslims did not receive pensions. Is that not a racist law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you that. Serbs didn't receive pensions either.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is whether you agree or whether you deny that in respect of that speech of mine during that commemoration, when I said that the Serbs were victimised because they were Serbs, are you denying that the independent state of Croatia had legalised killing on racial grounds of Serbs, Jews and Roma?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I am not aware of the existence of strict laws. I know that Serbs were being killed, but I don't know whether there were such laws that actually said, in writing, that it was permissible to kill Serbs. I don't know. Maybe that was the case, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the interview in "Borba," did you notice that it was the 16th of March of 1992, that that's when I gave that interview, that is, two days before the 18th of March, when the Lisbon Agreement was approved by the Serbs, Croats and Muslims of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I did not pay attention to the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point in time, did all Serbs live in one state?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Slovenes, Macedonians, did they all not live in one state? Were they all not constituent peoples of Yugoslavia, living in a single state, until it was broken up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did they not all live in Yugoslavia, in a single state?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, they did, but they were not all in a single state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was a single state.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us pause. I'm just asking you whether, in 1918, Serbs achieved that objective. Croats, Muslims, Serbs, did they all not attain this same objective, did they all not live in the same state?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that was everybody's objective. I'm not sure that that was the objective of all the peoples involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned my speech, and you say that I said that the Muslims would disappear. This is a speech made on the 14th or 15th of October, when what was being voted upon was independence or the Serbian vote against independence. Did I not say that there was a danger involved for Muslims, because if there were to be a war, Muslims could not defend themselves from Serbs and Croats; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am saying: Are you referring to that particular speech of mine?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to that particular speech of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to the examination-in-chief. You said that as for Muslims and Croats who would stay in the Serbian constituent unit, they would feel bad about it, and I can understand that. However, can you understand that a million and a half Serbs feel bad about being separated from Yugoslavia and living in Alija's Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, the same feelings that you recognise among the Muslims and Croats? Do you accept that the same kind of fears and anxieties were felt by Serbs if they were to be separated from Yugoslavia and if they were to live in a sovereign, unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina under Muslim domination?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: First of all, at that time no one said that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a unitary state. These are your dark expectations. So this is not Izetbegovic's Bosnia-Herzegovina. He is not the owner of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He cannot behave like the owner of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the owner of those three peoples. So these are just dark expectations. In life, there are problems, and problems are resolved in life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just intervene. The transcript does not reflect that the witness said that he knows that we, the Serbs, did not find a unitary Bosnia to be suitable, that it did not suit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that for the transcript, that you said that a unitary Bosnia did not suit the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, do you accept that on the 16th of March, two days before the agreement was concluded, we have been conducting talks for about ten months, negotiations on what the future Bosnia would be like, and we had accepted for Bosnia to leave Yugoslavia on the condition that it is not unitary?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That's the first time I hear of that, that you ever agreed to Bosnia-Herzegovina leaving Yugoslavia. I had never heard of that before, on the condition that it is not unitary. I mean, I've never heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I thought that this line of questioning about political topics was a bit unfair on you, because you were not really involved in that kind of thing. Do you agree that the essence of the Lisbon Agreement was that Bosnia would be independent, but that it would have three constituent units?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not that knowledgeable about politics, and I cannot really give you answers of a decided nature to such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But during the examination-in-chief, you were asked about preeminently political topics about which you had established your own views and opinions, especially on the basis of what you heard in the media and what you viewed in the coverage of Assembly sessions. On the basis of that, did you make some conclusions about political life?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, my questions were actually just focusing on the effect that such political speeches were held and maps were shown on the people that were living around the witness. I didn't ask him questions of a political nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's true, but also the witness mentioned his speech at the Assembly sessions. So with that caveat, I think the witness can answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat this. Witness, you watched Assembly sessions on television because they were broadcast, and on the basis of what you saw, you made your own assessments on how things were being interpreted in the public?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Again, you are reducing my answer only to the media, and now you're also reducing it only to Assembly sessions. I am a communicative person. I told you that I talked to many people, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, who are a bit more knowledgeable, as far as politics are concerned, more knowledgeable than I am, and you are trying to make me say that I formed my opinions on the basis of the media. And the media at the time were the ones that were poisoning the inter-ethnic relations. If someone was an objective observer, he had to read between the lines, as it were, and to try to discern the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you watch the Assembly session on the 24th and 25th of January, 1992, before the referendum took place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I am not familiar with what that particular session was. I watched Assembly sessions from time to time, but I cannot say that I watched all of them and throughout. Maybe I did watch that particular session. Perhaps you could remind me of what happened, but I cannot remember just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a session that is well known because Cengic and I went to the rostrum together and reached an agreement that lasted for about two hours. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up D87. This is a document that contains that speech of mine. The Serbian page is 104 and the English page is 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting : Do you remember that then I proposed that we wait with the referendum and for Bosnia to be regionalised, and then that we should have the referendum, the Serbs should have the referendum, and then Cengic, as the deputy prime minister, agreed to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I agree -- I remember that he agreed to something. I don't remember what your proposal was, but I do remember that at that point in time, you were close to some kind of agreement. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is the beginning of that speech. Can we look at page 106 in the Serbian and 102 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to start reading from the second paragraph: "Please, you cannot justify your wish to impose on us the independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, where you will rule over us, because we are not imposing anything on you. We are not asking that you remain in Yugoslavia. We are asking that Bosnia be transformed so that the Serbs maintain strong links with Yugoslavia, that Croats are not in any kind of link with Yugoslavia but have strong links with Croatia, and that Muslims have links both with Croatia and with Yugoslavia to the degree that they want; that is to say, a Serbian federation or whatever. It does not have to be called Yugoslavia." And then a little bit later: "The only way to do something together is to reorganise Bosnia and Herzegovina first so that it is acceptable to all three peoples. We are not going to impose anything on one another." Do you remember and do you agree that this was a reasonable position that opens the way for agreement and to avoid a conflict?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I do remember that there were constructive proposals from all three sides. However, the three of you were unable to reach any kind of agreement. Actually, I had the sense that you could have spoken for three more years together and you wouldn't have reached any kind of agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the Serbian page 107 and the English page 103 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to continue: "We will not impose anything on one another. We are not going to stop. We will work around the clock until we achieve such state organisation and such form which all three nations would be able to put their signature to, both Croats, Serbs and Muslims. Then we will hold a referendum that can be finished in 15 days. Gentlemen, that is the only way we can avoid an unwanted effect, that people calm down so that they can start living normally at last. Believe me, we have no influence over war or peace. The situation is very often out of control, and it happens always or very often that we could have control over such situations. "Gentlemen, all of you, including me, can picture now what would happen if, God forbid, unrests would start now or inter-ethnic and religious war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We could draw that on the board. Serbs would run away from Muslim areas, Muslims from the Serbian areas, and Croats would go to their areas. There would be shooting on the way, destruction of towns. There would be blood. And where would we find ourselves then? Serbs would be in Serbian areas, Muslims in the Muslim areas, and Croats in the Croatian areas, fully homogeneous. And what would we have to do? We would again have to sit down and agree and place all three signatures on that agreement, because without all three signatures, there is no solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina." Witness, did this actually happen, that I said would happen before the Assembly if no agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, a similar thing did happen, but I'm not sure what you built such dark thoughts on at that time, that there would be so much bloodshed and killing. It means that you already had some kind of perception about what sort of things would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- would you agree that a politician has to have perception, and to be able to predict what would happen, and to be very familiar with the situation in order to be able to make any predictions? Could anybody be a politician at all without being able to predict anything, not only keeping in mind World War II but also the mood among the masses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, that is one thing. But having such dark predictions and thoughts about killings at that scale, that is something else. I didn't hear about such dark predictions on the other two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree -- yes, I have to make some pauses. Do you agree that only the war that settled down or quietened down at the beginning of that month gave me an idea about what would happen in Bosnia, which was much more mixed in terms of population than Croatia was, as to what would happen in Bosnia if the war were to break out? I'm talking about the war in Croatia which had been soothed or calmed in the beginning of January or February 1992.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: And that is precisely why you should have used all of your mental and physical efforts to stop that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we agree there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Serbian page 108 and the English page 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read this paragraph: "Therefore, let us make -- let us make a Bosnia-Herzegovina the way it can be made, that Croats in every moment --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have doubts whether you have to read out all those passages; just you can introduce the crux of it. The witness can read it, we can read it. So think about a method in terms of reducing the reading-out time. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I just wanted this paragraph where you can see what my position was in relation to Croats, where I say: "Let us create Bosnia-Herzegovina in the way it can be, that Croats at every moment are not lost for Croatia, that they have links, their representatives in Zagreb as well as their representatives in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that now Croats from Bosnia can vote in Croatia and they vote in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't think that that is quite right, that they can both vote in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did they exercise that right, even though you think that that is not quite right? That is what they want and that is how they do things?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, that is what they do, but that doesn't make it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to conclude with this topic: Are these efforts to reach a solution, as you said earlier? You said that all three of us or all three leaders -- you are thinking of the three parties, the three leaders, the three ethnic communities -- was this an effort to come to a solution, all the more so because Muhamed Cengic, as you recall, had accepted that, and there was the conviction that there would be the regionalisation first and then the referendum?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the end, Cengic says: "Sir, we agreed like this, and let us conclude together, the two of us, let us do that before all of these people." So Mr. Cengic accepted that, and then after the break somebody intervened for that agreement to fall through. So had we regionalised Bosnia-Herzegovina and held the referendum together, and had received what Ambassador Cutileiro had recommended and what was finally granted at Dayton, would that have been a solution without bloodshed and without war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We are now going to move to things that you could have seen. I'm going to go through these questions briefly. You were in the JNA for 11 months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you a cook, by your specialty, and did you have any additional specialties?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Can you please remind me what this military specialty means, "Ves," V-e-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Ves," I don't know exactly. I think it's your specialty, occupational military specialty.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, I was -- I was a quarter-master. I was in that military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in your "Ves," V-e-s, you would have been a cook?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I did not have the job of a cook in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I read somewhere that that was your training. Is it correct that during those 11 months, you had general training in the period of three to five months?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: We had training for three months, training to be cooks. You are correct there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you go through military training, which included professional training, physical training, and political training?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any physical training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The military professional part had to do with personal and collective weaponry up to the level of platoon and a company, tactical training, the actions of individuals in combat, and then specialist training on the basis of the occupational specialty; is that true?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, we had short infantry training, familiarisation with weapons, and then in the meantime also cooking skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As part of your political training and education, you covered the socio-political system, international relations, and moral training?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. It was political and morale training, that's what it was called. Probably it did include all of those things. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As part of that, you also covered international relations, International Humanitarian Law, military -- Laws of War and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, then, that would have been the only unit that would have not had that in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't recall any kind of training or lectures on international relations or International Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you receive the Rules of Service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: What are you specifically thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After training, did you get a booklet of the rules that every soldier, military man, would need to know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: What is a booklet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a small training manual, a manual.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, we didn't get anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, that, again, would be a singular case.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There were 80 of us in the company. I am not the only one that didn't get that. The Rules of Service were mentioned, but this booklet that you referred to is something that none of us were given. I'm not that senile to have forgotten that. I had been issued a booklet, I would have had a booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Rules of Service in the JNA during your training?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: To a certain degree, this was discussed. I couldn't really tell you exactly. Rules of Service were referred to frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, the conduct of a soldier is based on the Rules of Service, and if Rules of Service are violated, you have to accept the consequences. So you had to have been informed about the Rules of Service in the JNA; is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: We were probably informed about it. We were learning about the Rules of Service, although the commanders, themselves, did not strictly adhere to these Rules of Service in the ideal way as you would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were transferred to the reserve forces. You received your military booklet, your combat wartime assignment, but you were not on the schedule according to any other occupational specialty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes. Luckily, that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that people who were summoned for exercises frequently took their uniforms, gas masks, and some of them even their infantry weaponry home with them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware that they had their infantry weapons with them. That would be left in the barracks. The weapons were not taken home. As for the uniforms and the gas masks, yes, some people did have them at home. I'm not aware that anyone actually had weapons at home, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you reported to the military at Grbavica, you handed your military booklet to them, and for a short period of time they kept it, for a few days, and they then returned it to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was quite clear, from the military booklet, that you are a soldier who had gone through training and that you were in the reserve forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Having seen your military booklet, it was clear to them that you had served your military term of duty, that you were a trained soldier, and that you had been transferred to the reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, you could have seen that from the military booklet. There was a stamp indicating that I had completed my regular term of duty in the JNA. You could see that. You could see the military post, the place where I served my term of duty, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the main reason -- actually, another question first. Would you agree that the national parties managed to overthrow Communists from power in a kind of partnership or a coalition, and that before the elections, those three parties agreed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I just take a short break? I apologise. Please forgive me. Could you please repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the three parties went for elections, with the goal of changing the system, and that together they overthrew the Communists?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: It wasn't quite clear to me what the goals were of those nationalist parties. I, personally, did not like that indication, national or nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's be specific. In your view, what was the reason for the escalation of tension within the Assembly or in political life? What was the key event that led to the rising or the increase of tensions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There is no key event, in my mind, or a key point in time for this increase of tensions. Tensions were getting stronger for a long series of years. It's not something that happened suddenly and suddenly there was tension. Tensions were in Yugoslavia since Slobodan Milosevic came to power in Serbia. That is the first time that these tensions surfaced, disagreements, different opinions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I could say now that he came to power because tensions existed before him, but I'm not going to go into that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Witness: Did the secession of two republics, Slovenia and Croatia, and later on Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, was that the main topic and the main event at all Assembly sessions, their secession?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, you can are omitting to mention that with the arrival of Slobodan Milosevic to power, the existence of two socialist autonomous provinces was brought to an end prior to that. The Constitution of the SFRY clearly spells out which parts comprised the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There were six republics and two autonomous provinces. So the balance had already been disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are political topics. We will not go into that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You are the one touching upon politics. You promised to me that we would not go into politics, and you constantly lead us that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you agree, then, that the tensions -- or, rather, that the mobilisation of reservists in 1991 was linked to the war in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: In a certain way, yes, because that condition reflected upon Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the inter-ethnic relations deteriorated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was mostly Muslims and Croats who refused to attend regular mobilisation exercises or join regular forces, and that only the Serb community remained loyal to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The Serbs from urban areas also refused to join the JNA. It was only rural Serbs who joined the army. The Serbs from Sarajevo were not very keen on going to these exercises and responding to mobilisation. Most of them refused. There were some who did join, but most of them refused to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That would then be described as -- or, rather, that could be expressed with one of our sayings, that a rich man will send a bull to the army, whereas a poor man will send his son. Have you switched your phone off?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I thought I did, but apparently I didn't, and I apologise once again. I switched it off now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that huge JNA resources had to be withdrawn from Slovenia, and then later on they withdrew from a large part of Croatia, that is to say, from the two-thirds of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, they did withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They withdrew to the remaining parts of Yugoslavia, where they considered that they needed to defend the territory, to defend that part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know what considerations they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now enumerate the facilities held by the JNA, the infrastructure of the JNA, in Sarajevo and in the vicinity so that we can see why they had such huge resources there? And you can just confirm what you know, and what you don't know, just say so. It was the Command of the 2nd Military District that was headquartered there; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Command of the 4th Corps, barracks in Lukavica, Barracks Viktor Bubanj. I'm just going to enumerate them, and you can tell me for which ones you disagree. Viktor Bubanj Barracks, the barracks in Halilovici, Marsal Tito Barracks, Jajce Barracks, barracks in Butile, barracks in Pale, barracks in Pazarici, military factories in Vogosca, Famos Hrasnica, Famos Pale, factory ORAO in Rajlovac, repair workshop in Hadzici. They also partially owned a factory called Zrat. Would you agree that all of this was the JNA infrastructure in Sarajevo and in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the vicinity of Sarajevo. However, that's not where the problem lies. The problem lies in the fact that it was the weapons that were withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia that were distributed exclusively to Serbs before the war broke out. This is something that I learned during the war from the people who were with me. That's where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will get to that eventually. Would you agree with me that the JNA lacked manpower for that amount of weapons and that it had to provide weapons for its reservists? And you were one of the reservists. The JNA had to ensure that it had enough reservists that it could call upon, if needed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That wasn't my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some Croats and some Muslims responded to mobilisation, and that those who did respond had access to weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that two Croats held senior positions in the Command of Sarajevo Romanija Corps all the way up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us focus on the chaos that, according to you, ruled in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this time for our break or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll take a break. We'll break for half an hour, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin, do you have something to raise with us before you continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wish to say I would kindly ask to go into closed session, please. Mr. Karadzic, via his questions, indirectly reveals my identity and my ethnic background, although in the beginning he was warned not to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us just explore a bit further this chaotic period in your neighbourhood. Is this settlement a part of Novo Sarajevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that some people gladly responded to the call to join reserve forces and some other people only pretended to do that and wore uniforms as though they had joined the reserve forces; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, there was such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those who faked to have responded, did they also have weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in Bosnia, a long time before the war, one could buy, rather cheaply, some weapons, small arms?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: What do you mean by "small arms"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to a pistol, a rifle, PA -- semi-automatic rifle, and so on.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that easy or cheap to buy it. It wasn't that easily available for purchase. It wasn't at each corner, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see what other places people could procure weapons from, other than the JNA and the police. Is it true that local communes, or factories, et cetera, had their own Territorial Defence units and they had their own stocks of weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, they did have weapons, but they were kept in the TO warehouses, which were within the JNA warehouses. So there were no weapons kept in companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that there was some smuggling and that one could buy a rifle, or a semi-automatic rifle, or a so-called PASP rifle with a sniper; perhaps not cheaply, but it was available?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, it's not true that snipers could be purchased, at least not to my knowledge. I know that the Serbs used to sell weapons they had received, the ones that you are mentioning, semi-automatic rifles, rifles and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a group that had mortars. Did you say that that group wore cockades as their insignia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't remember that they had cockades. They did wear uniforms, but I'm not sure about cockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's in your statement, and if we have time, we will revert to that. In your statement, you also said -- in your 1997 statement, on page 4, you said that there were no serious preparations for war conducted in Bosnia, even though on page 4 you say: "Naturally, all of these events in Croatia had direct influence on the situation in Bosnia. In addition to that, it was clear that the authorities were not aware of what was about to happen to us and what grave consequences would ensue. This is why no serious preparations for war were conducted." Did you know that, nevertheless, there were serious preparations for war conducted, if not by the state, then by the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D28070.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it: You said that Serbs took Grbavica without firing a single bullet; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you reported, you received a uniform, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were given weapons and a patch; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I got a semi-automatic rifle. What do you mean by "patch"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get something that would mark your affiliation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that you said somewhere in your statement that you were given a flag.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Later, but not at that moment when I was given weapons. I think that this patch with a Serb flag was something that we received later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D28070.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that there were almost 2.000 organised Green Berets of the Patriotic League before the war had broken out, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Novo Sarajevo. I'm repeating it so that the transcript would reflect it, Novo Sarajevo. Could you please look at the first page of the document. It can be displayed to the public because it has nothing to do with the witness. You see that General Delic here is providing a survey of the patriotic forces of the resistance that were there when the aggression started, as he says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have two, three, four, five -- the fifth page of this document. It's fine in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this highlighted part: "Regional Staff of the Patriotic League, Sarajevo. "Regional Staff of the Patriotic League and Green Berets for the Sarajevo region consolidated and connected organisationally and at the same time subordinated, organised forces of the PO BiH and Green Berets that were formed in all municipalities of the region. At municipal level, these units, from squad level to company and detachment level, were subordinated to municipal staffs that guided their activities." So here is a review for the different municipalities in the city.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. I think that it is fine in English. Actually, no, we need the next page in English too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the municipality of Novo Sarajevo: "Composition of Municipal Staff of the TO Staff of Novo Sarajevo on the 18th of April, 1992. "Twenty-three active and reserve officers." And: "1.730 soldiers." And the total is 1.753. "Four detachments. "Three independent companies. "Three independent platoons." As for weapons, they had 450 small arms. Do you think that this was not reason enough for the Serbs to be concerned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I was not there in the army, so I cannot talk to you about that. You know, I was in Grbavica, that's where I was in the area. What was going on over there, that is something I don't know, so I wouldn't know what was happening on the Serb side had I not been there. You see, I cannot talk about what happened on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Karadzic, the 65 ter number of this document is 1D2807, without "0" at the end, and I don't see the name of General Delic in this document. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Excellency. This was sent to Delic. This is a report sent to Delic. Delic had asked for it in order to compile a history of the establishment of their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, Witness, on the 18th of April, this is part of the total preparations of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. These preparations started from the 31st of March and then went on to the 13th of April. Then there was this public meeting on the 10th of June, I believe, in 1991. So I'm not talking about their side and our side. I'm talking about the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, all of it. We are going to have a look at the map of that area later, but this is Novo Sarajevo, including Grbavica. Had you known this, would you have been concerned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, if it says here that 1.730 soldiers are available and they have only 450 rifles, they're not really very well armed. It seems that one out of three soldiers had a rifle, one out of three soldiers had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you had shifts? You would work for 12 hours, and then you would be resting for 24 hours; that's what you did most of the time; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Most of the time. Not always, but most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if a rifle remains in the trenches, then every soldier who is on the front-line has a rifle, because one-third are on the front-line and two-thirds are not there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, but then we have 450 armed soldiers, not 1.730.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, this is before the beginning of the war. This is before the army was established. That is to say, that they were already part of the Territorial Defence as an established unit before the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has clearly said that he does not know anything about the other side, what they have and how they were organised, so I don't see that he can be the basis for such a document. Therefore, the Prosecution objects.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this document speaks about the witness's claims and his knowledge. If he doesn't know that, he could not have made the claims he did in his statements. This preeminently has to do with the topics dealt with in the statement and the examination-in-chief. It shows specifically that the assessment to the effect that the Serbs had no cause for concern there were not true. As we continue, you will see that there was fighting, heavy fighting at that, in Grbavica, which the witness, mercifully, had not seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You put your question in relation to this document, which is already on the record, and you will have another opportunity to tender this and admit this. So I don't think this witness is a proper basis to admit this. You know the practice. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Witness, do you realise that you missed a lot if you did not know that the Patriotic League had almost 2.000 soldiers in your very own municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: As I said, you're talking about 2.000 soldiers, but there are 450 armed soldiers there. When I say "soldier," I mean a soldier with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wish to ask you whether your position would have been somewhat different had you been aware of the secret organisation of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Which position do you mean, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I read it. It was on page 4, you thought that no preparations were carried out for the war, whereas I claimed -- the Defence claims that preparations were underway, preparations for war, and that that happened in 103 municipalities. Out of 109, 103 municipalities had municipal staffs of the Patriotic League established already in the beginning of 1991 and about 100.000 soldiers placed under a command. On page 14, you say there was no resistance in Grbavica, they took it without a single gun-shot being fired. Now the Defence has to put to you the actual situation as it was. I'm dealing with your statements now, and I would like to give you this opportunity to realise what the actual situation was. So I'm asking you whether you realised that in your very own municipality, there was this secret military organisation called the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, and it doesn't really matter what quantities of weapons.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I can tell you, with full responsibilities, that in Grbavica there was no fighting or there was no resistance before the Serb forces arrived there. I'm sure of that 100 per cent. I saw that with my very own eyes. Grbavica is part of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we now have 1D2781. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am going to put this to you now. It's on the 14th of April that this news agency is reporting that the Public Security building of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo were transferred to the premises of the Forestry Engineering School Centre at Omladinsko Setaliste: "The goal of such regrouping of this fundamentalist military hoard is control over intersections of Bratstvo-Jedinstvo and Omladinsko Setaliste, intersections at the tram station Pofalici and the surroundings of Grbavica." Do you agree that the municipality of Novo Sarajevo has a Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You're talking about the population, aren't you? The municipality of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that Muslim policemen were transferred to the Muslim part of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo and that they established a new station there with a view to having these intersections under their control, and that was the situation until the end of the war; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That's not right. The former Public Security Station is still on the territory that would later be under their control during the war, when the war broke out as well. That is to say that -- that is to say that both locations were on the other side of the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That just means that the Serbs did not take what these people had left or abandoned; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, they did not take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript does not reflect that you confirmed that Novo Sarajevo was a municipality with a majority Serb population. So could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I think that the majority population was Serb and that during these first so-called democratic elections, the Serb Democratic party won a majority in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, we don't see any basis to admit this through this witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2782, can we have that, please. The Defence believes that this speaks of the same topics, but it's on the basis of documents that show that there had been fighting and that the situation was different from what the witness had observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this, Witness. The 21st of April, this is what "SRNA" says: "'SRNA' has found that severe fighting has been carried out since morning in Sarajevo. The conflict focus point was previously located in Grbavica area, however, later it spread to other localities in town. The Muslim paramilitary forces open fire towards positions of Serbian defenders at Vraca from the mortar fire from Hum, as well as from Elektroprivreda building and Sociona [phoen] building where the sniper shooters of the Green Berets are located." Did you see or hear that in April, shells were falling on Vraca and that snipers were operating?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
