utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not going to admit this either; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2783, can we have that, please. This is a document, or, rather, agency news, the 25th of April: "'SRNA' has found out that over 1.000 Muslim paramilitary forces launched an attack against the Serb settlement of Vraca from the direction of Zlatiste and Colina Kapa at 1945 hours. Numerous Muslim units are also penetrating from the direction of Grbavica. These units, in their fierce attack, destroyed Serb houses within a circle around the Jewish cemetery, as well as above the neighbourhood of Kovaci."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that Grbavica was in Muslim hands at that point in time and that they were attacking Vraca from there, and Colina Kapa and Zlatiste were in their hands too? And Colina Kapa was under Muslim control throughout the war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I don't know about Zlatiste belonging to Grbavica. Perhaps it is the municipality of Sarajevo, but it's not Grbavica. You know full well what Grbavica is. Zlatiste is not Grbavica. Colina Kapa is not Grbavica either. You keep trying to put some different regions under the heading of "Grbavica," but that is simply not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was too fast and I was not paying enough attention. The Serb neighbourhood of Vraca, do we agree that it is a Serb neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: We do not agree. Why would Vraca be a Serb neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Vraca inhabited by over 80 per cent of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, especially not since the new buildings were built in the Petrovacka Street area. So it's not really true that there are over 80 per cent of Serbs at Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about 50 per cent? Were there more than 50 per cent of Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am saying, on the basis of this item, that it was attacked from the direction of Zlatiste and Colina Kapa, from the direction of Grbavica. I'm not saying that that is Grbavica, but do you agree that Colina Kapa throughout the whole period remained in Muslim hands?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but there were never attacks staged from the Grbavica area. That is not true. That would imply attacks from the other Miljacka bank, which -- that, what you're saying, and that's just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the attack have been launched from the Zeljo Stadium from Grbavica II area from Strojorad? Is that also Grbavica, and could an attack have been launched from there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: It could have been, but it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is all of this on the left bank of the Miljacka River, where the Serb part of the town is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You mean the Strojorad area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Zeljo Stadium?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this going to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, apart from the ethnic composition of those areas, are you or were you aware of the 1.000 Muslim paramilitary forces attack against Vraca from the direction of Zlatiste and Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, like I'm saying, that is not strictly the Grbavica area, but I'm not really -- I wasn't there. I cannot speak of things that I didn't see for myself. There was combat in the Zlatiste area. At the beginning of the war, Zlatiste was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then after that Serbs took control of that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't see any basis to admit this document, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D2806, please. And we are going to see an intercept -- an intercepted telephone conversation between General Milutin Kukanjac and General Mandzic of the 21st of April. At the same time, this news agency speaks about the two JNA generals to which the Serbs are objecting because they failed to protect them. I don't know if there's a translation. We don't have a translation right now, and I'm going to read slowly: "Mandzic here." And then he is connected to General Kukanjac. And then in the middle, it says: "Let me tell you, I have been listening to these explosions from this morning, and I can't ..." And then there is a swear word, and then Kukanjac says: "Everybody's firing." Mandzic says: "Another thing. I have some retired people and some relatives in that area, and according to what they say, these guys are attacking from the left bank, Miljacka." Kukanjac says: "Yes." Mandzic: "With the objective of capturing something over there. I think this is a forceful solution of the question of the division of Sarajevo." Can we look at the next page, please. And then they swear -- General Mandzic swears, and then he says: "What can be done to stop this? My heart is heavy ..." And so on and so forth. And then he says: "This is banditry, the worst kind of terrorism." And then Kukanjac says: "I called both Koljevic and Karadzic and all of these Muslim leaders. Look, they're firing from Hum, these Muslims. They're firing from Crni Vrh, they're firing from Marin Dvor, they're firing from Zlatiste, and these from Vraca have entered town. This is awful." And then a little bit later, it says: "This Karic is lying over the radio, saying nonsense, that we have tanks down there, this is nothing to do with the truth." Karic is lying, Karic, not Karadzic: "Karic was a 'Vehbija,' and he was recently under the command of Kukanjac, and then he left the JNA. And then Kukanjac says -- Mandzic is asking him: "This is clear to me. Is it possible that there are these Seselj's men there?" And Kukanjac says: "No." Mandzic says: "And ..." Kukanjac says: "I don't think so. You know them. In order to justify things, it's easy for them to say Seselj's or Arkan's men. There are none of those men in Sarajevo, no."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you understand now that these two generals confirm that there are explosions everywhere and that there was a heavy exchange of fire? Muslims are firing from Hum, from Marin Dvor, from Crni Vrh, above the military hospital and from Zlatiste, and the Serbs from Vraca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, I don't understand that, but that is not really correct at all. I lived in Grbavica, and there were no shells dropping around my building, no snipers shooting either, or shells, nothing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But Vraca was not far away, and you can hear explosions. Did you hear explosions that day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You could hear explosions, but it's difficult, if you don't see it with your own eyes, to assess whether these are just fired from there or if it was fired from the other side and explodes in Vraca. I did pass through Vraca, and I wasn't really able to see the shells falling. You cannot hide that if you -- if shells drop, you cannot hide that. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I have to tell you that this is a good example how you are wasting your time. The witness already said he's not aware of the situation in Vraca that took place at the time. Reading out these intercepts does not form any part of your evidence. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one more question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far is Vraca from Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: From where I lived, it's approximately 6, 7 to 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Grbavica leads on to Vraca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm not going to tender this. I'm going to tender it at some other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. These are two confirmations that on the 21st of April, there was fierce fighting that you failed to notice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 30714, please. We have a translation as well. This is an intercept between me and the other Radovan, Radovan Pejic, who is a prominent MUP official, and I'm asking him here: "Is that Vraca?" And they respond. And Karadzic says: "Good afternoon. We are working here. We are having negotiations." And he says: "It's quiet at the moment." And then he says: "Except for the fact that we are in the position because there are some indications that they keep getting organised down there in Grbavica, are getting organised." In the English, can we look at the next page, please: "They are getting organised in Grbavica." And then it says: "There was some attacks from that area last night, and so -- yes, we are just getting ready so that we can defend ourselves in case they start attacking us again." And then I say: "All right. We should sign ... the cease-fire today, and therefore we should not -- we must not initiate any attacks, and they should not do so either."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that on this page? This is an intercept that was recorded or picked up by the Muslim police. Do you see that the police knows that they are getting organised in Grbavica to attack Vraca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I lived in Grbavica, and I never saw a single soldier in Grbavica either from the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, never. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic says -- Karadzic is asking: "Did you have any damage?" And then Pejic says: "Our premises were shelled yesterday and the day before yesterday, and the windows in the canteen are all cracked due to the detonations around the premises, so we're forced to be using the other entrance. All of that was burning." Do you know where the school -- the police school is in Vraca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you admit this intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the basis of the witness's knowledge where the school was? We don't see any basis, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D2805 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report from the MUP to the prime minister, dated the 30th of April. Let's look at the bottom, the paragraph that begins with: "Pripadnici." "Members of the TO BiH from the region of the Grbavica Stadium, where the bulk of these forces is concentrated, fired all night from automatic weapons and snipers at buildings of the Serbian MUP." Do you allow for the possibility that this was so?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Since it is not stated here where the buildings of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior are -- where is that located so that the Muslims are firing on that? Where exactly is that in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The school.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: In Vraca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Which period is this that we're talking about, which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you see at the bottom, where it says: "From the elementary school, Ivan Goran Kovacic, at the Pere Kosorica Square, fire was opened at facilities of the Serbian MUP and the Vraca Memorial Park from automatic weapons, Zoljas, Ocas [phoen] and snipers." Do you know where this school, Ivan Goran Kovacic, is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I know where it is, and if you know where it is, then it would be clear and logical to you that no weapons could be fired from that school in the direction of Vraca. If you're at the school or on top of the school, you are facing the high-rise buildings on the Pere Kosorica Square, so you could not be able to hit Vraca. Also, a Zolja does not have the range to strike at Vraca from Ivan Goran Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. We are not going to be tendering this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you receive -- when you received your combat disposition or assignment, you said that it was difficult to pass between the high-rise buildings. At the time that you were in Grbavica, until (redacted), were there any barriers, obstacles, reinforcements, containers, and even curtains across the street from sheets and blankets in order to shield ones from sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the map. It doesn't have to be in closed -- private session until we move to some more specific things. Let's look at the map that shows New Sarajevo. I'm going to do this so that the parties and the Trial Chamber can clearly see what this municipality looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you completely dispute the fact that at this time, there was fighting that these reports refer to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I am saying, again, I'm not disputing it. It's just that I'm not aware that there was anything. I'm not aware. I wasn't at Zlatiste, I wasn't in this other location - I forget the name of it - above Grbavica. I wasn't there. But I did hear that there was fighting at Zlatiste. I could hear it, I could hear the fighting. I didn't see it, though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P815. The map was admitted as P815.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to take the pencil that the service will show you and circle the New Sarajevo -- Novo Sarajevo municipality. And then later I'm going to ask you to mark the map some more. It reaches all the way to the top of Hum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, I'm finding it difficult to find my way on this map. Is it possible to zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe we can zoom in on the central part. But do you see it? It says "Municipality Novo Sarajevo." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see these boundaries?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there's no need to mark the map. Do you agree that at the top, on the north side of the map, going from the inhabited area, there is this inhabited area to the north, and then towards Hum, that is where the Serbian settlement of Pofalici lies, that is a 100 per cent Serb-inhabited settlement of Pofalici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, that's the settlement of Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you mark that place with the letter P, "P" for "Pofalici"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that this part here is Pofalici [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is right, thank you. Do you know that until the 15th of May, between 250 to 300 Serbs were killed, and almost all of their houses were torched?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know how many Serbs were killed, and if they were killed, whether houses were burned or not. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this was in all of the media. Did you hear from the media that Serbs, all those who had stayed to live in that area, were killed and routed out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. It's possible that there were some killings, but I'm not sure that it's possible that all of them were killed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know about any Serbs being killed in Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know any specific examples. I wasn't there, and I don't know of any acquaintances, friends, or any personalities living there. It's possible, but I simply didn't hear of it. In my statement, I said that in the Grbavica part of town, there were no -- there was no fighting when the VRS entered Novo Sarajevo municipality and Grbavica, that there was no combat when the Serbian Army entered Grbavica. And as for Pofalici, I only heard of it. I'm simply not aware of it. I didn't live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see Grbavica here. We can see both front-lines. We can see the hinterland behind Grbavica, and these are mostly Serb villages in this area; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Which area do you have in mind as being predominantly Serbian? You mean the hinterland behind Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a letter G where Grbavica is and letter V where Vraca is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "G" stands for "Grbavica" and that entire flatland, and then Vraca is up on the hill; am I right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that here, further in, we can see Lukavica and then that this other area around it is almost 100 per cent populated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Predominantly Serb settlements; not 100 per cent, but predominantly Serb. There was some Croats and Muslims there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But up there in the mountain area, if you remember Trivkovici, Zivkovici, Biocici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Pandurevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mostly Serb villages; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please put an L where Lukavica is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Is this Lukavica here [marks]? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, could you please date this and sign with your initials so that this can be admitted into evidence and we can move to another map. Just put a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your initial being your witness number, which is KDZ310, 310.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the date. You started writing "29th."

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, could we see another document from the month of June, 1D2792. And then we will move into a closed session to see this map in detail. 1D2792.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that on the 8th of June, an all-out offensive began, Muslim offensive, in the Sarajevo area, and in all parts of the town, on all front-lines, there was fierce fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at this news coming in from agencies, where it reads, according to the information coming in from the news agencies, the attack that started in the morning continued until the afternoon, and the last sentence says: "The same source states that in Grbavica II, infantry combat is in progress." Is Grbavica II that far away from you that you didn't know that there was any fighting going on there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There was no fighting going on there. I know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. In that case, we will not offer this into evidence. Could we now move into closed session, because I'm about to ask the witness to mark some locations on a more detailed map. Could we see 09390C on the 65 ter list, and we need Map 11. This is number 9. We need number 11, please, sheet 11. Are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not yet. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 1081.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described that chaotic situation very nicely. From the beginning of April until mid-May, practically no one knew who was in power in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There were no troops in Grbavica, so I cannot say that it was under Serb control, or under Muslim control, or under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that that is when criminals had their chance, and that crime reigned in the area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were no criminals in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There wasn't any looting at that time at all. There was no looting, there were no expulsions of people from their homes. There was no looting. Cars were not being taken from people. It's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that. I'm just asking you in general, not only until the 15th of May. In that period, were there any criminals there? Actually, do you remember that criminals had developed a new business, as it were, secretly taking people from one side to the other?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You mean the period before Grbavica was taken by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Later on as well. On the whole.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Before the Serbs came to Grbavica, anybody could have crossed to the other side of the Miljacka River, so there could have been no business of transferring people from this side to that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Serbs came" --

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I mean the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Organised army. Was the JNA there all the time at Lukavica, in Transit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Before Grbavica was taken, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There were JNA units, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention now to this document. This is a document which is a report for the commissioner of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, from the Crisis Staff. He is reporting to the president of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he says: "Over the past two months in the territory of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the following activities have been carried out: "A crisis staff has been set up ..." And then he says which local communes were included, Grbavica, Vraca, Hrasno, Brdo, Lukavica, Tilava, and so on. And: "This crisis staff is performing the function of the Municipal Assembly in war conditions." Now, 3(a), "Accommodation," do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This has to do with putting up people who have no homes, and now B says: "Food supplies. "Local communes have made lists of civilians, including their first and last names, and food was provided to families of fighters and refugees from occupied territory." Can we move on to the next page, please. Do you see this, "Army Food Supplies," and then "Health Care and Medical Corps," an infirmary was turned into an emergency centre, the health centre has about 15 employees and so on? Now look at this sentence: "In local communes, 19 vehicles (cadets and five-ton trucks) have been assigned to the Medical Corps to be used as ordered by the head of the Medical Corps." At one point, you described that the soldiers asked someone for a car; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: They did not ask for a car. They asked for the keys to take the car away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in wartime, a private vehicle can also be requisitioned for army purposes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, but not on ethnic grounds, not only to requisition vehicles of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know exactly how many vehicles were taken, and do you know what the ethnic structure was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many vehicles were taken, but vehicles were being taken from the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any Serb whose vehicle had been seized?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you claim that no Serb's vehicle was seized?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at F.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, they asked me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I see. Please, can this be deleted? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, have a look at F. The Executive Board restricted the prices of food supplies.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: You said F?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: F. Do you see F, "Shops"? "The Crisis Staff and the Executive Board have allowed the MIS supermarket in Grbavica to sell goods, but at prices set by the Executive Board." So that is to say that they did not allow any wheeling and dealing in that area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: But this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next page. The translation is incorrect here. It's not treatment of Muslims and Croats, but relation or attitude towards Muslims and Croats. "Relation towards Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if you can look at this paragraph in the Serbian, and the rest in the English: "Citizens of all nationalities assemble frequently, especially in Grbavica, and our public attitude is very correct. We appoint a head of every building, who is responsible for the situation in his building and for all the information about the occupants. Secretly, the police apply the usual procedure to people who are engaged in military activities against us. "We have informed the Muslims that they would be safe if they were militarily neutral in relation to us, and so far the situation has been good. "We visited the nunnery in Gornji Kovacici and discussed co-operation, loyalty and the nuns' safety with them." Did you know that this nunnery remained in Grbavica throughout the whole time tranquil and safe?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you allow for that possibility; is that correct ?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: It's not like that. The nuns were actually expelled to the other side, and it's not correct that the police had superintendents in each building. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I know because there were some people who had organised themselves at the special blocks and entrances to buildings, but when the police came, they explicitly banned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We have evidence on that, and we will leave that for later. When did the nuns leave, and who expelled them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that this was not correct and that all of their treasures were safeguarded and handed them over at the end of the war, the whole library of the Theological Faculty and from that part as well, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: It's possible that the library and the things were safeguarded, but the nuns were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When, what day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but they were expelled right at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with this easily. Look at paragraph 7 here now. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Robbery and theft." This commissioner, this gentleman, is reporting that: "These have been rife, especially car thefts. We are almost powerless here, and there is not much we can do about this because this is the responsibility of the military and civilian police ." So he's reporting that crime was rife. Do you agree with this assessment of his?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: What period is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He's reporting on the 5th of June for the two months that had just passed, April and May.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There was mass looting from the point in time when the Serbian Army entered Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you ascribed that to the military?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: To the military police, the army, and the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were a part of that army. Did you loot?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Not all Serbian soldiers looted. In order to make a house, you need a lot of people. In order to knock it down, you only need one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber which unit did the looting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Soldiers and policemen from different units looted, those who were at the lines, those from the intervention platoons, those who were in the civilian police, those who were in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we dispute this and we know that this was not so, and we will call those people to testify here - if you need to say this in private session, we'll go into private session - can you please tell the Trial Chamber the names of the persons who looted -- headed the people or led the people who looted, or did not stop that, or issued such orders?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: There was no order to loot. Everybody looted as they wished. There were people who did the looting. There were also honest soldiers and people who did not do that -- that I know did not do that for sure. I know soldiers from my unit who were honest, who did not steal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time to have a break. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 1.00, after which you will have about 50 minutes to conclude your cross-examination. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a person who at that point is exercising his power, and he says that he's unable to put an end to the looting. And we will see when that happened. Can you please look at item number 8 now, "Accommodation of Fighters From Other Areas." "For those fighters who have joined regular units, we provide accommodation in empty and deserted Croatian and Muslim flats. We give them permission to use those flats temporarily, and they assume the obligation to take care of the furniture." Did you know about cases like that, where people were permitted to temporarily use an apartment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The permission was given. I'm not sure whether it was for temporary use. As for whether they looked after the furniture and what was in the apartment, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me of a single case where a person who was issued an apartment that had all its contents recorded, that he abused it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: What sort of a list of things that were there? You mean he received an apartment with a list of all the things that were there? What do you want me to do, give you the name of such a person?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like you to tell me of a case when a person to whom a commission had issued the permission to use an apartment destroyed the contents of that apartment.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, one of those people would be Zoran Colic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the apartment issued to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Zoran Colic. He was issued an apartment, and he looted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He looted it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. We will call him to testify.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, you cannot call him because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last paragraph, where this gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you want to say something about Mr. Colic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- we perhaps have to go into private session for these details. I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into private session, if you so wish. Yes, we'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the last paragraph, where this gentleman, who is a representative of the authorities, he says: "We also request that this report be treated as official, and that the entire government treat it as such, so as to prevent any rumours, misinformation, and intentional or unintentional false reports. Any other individual oral reports and interpretations are merely the personal opinions of people and do not have the character of official assessments." And now, Witness, sir, this man who is exercising his authority there accepts the situation where there are some occurrences that he's not able to deal with, does not have the documents. On page 4 -- one, two, three, four -- page 4. Can we go back to the previous 4, page 4, where he says that this cannot be -- this is paragraph 3 on page 4, where he says: "We cannot objectively manage to do all the work there is because virtually nothing can be done without a network of local communes." So his assessment is similar to yours, that there are such occurrences, and so on and so forth, but he, as a representative of the authorities, says that he does not have the possibility of putting an end to all of that. Earlier, you said that there were no orders for looting, that this was done by soldiers. Was this looting done by an organised unit, pursuant to instructions, or was this looting done by soldiers in their free time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I had the sense that the expulsions were carried out pursuant to orders. As for the looting, directly, there was no command or an instruction by some commander or something. You know, things were looted, money, gold, cars, and then it went from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D885, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we're dealing with expulsions, let us clarify that matter. You say that until the 15th of May, more or less, you could freely cross over, before the lines were set up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Before the Serbian Army came to Grbavica. Afterwards, you could also cross over, but it got more and more difficult, and in the end you could not cross over anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So when was the expulsion carried out, then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: People were expelled from the time the Serbian Army came to Grbavica and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. And when I tell you that a bird could not pass -- first of all, the journalists were running away, then there was the Muslim Army that was firing when people were crossing over, so how can you explain a mass expulsion after the lines were set up, when a bird was not -- unable to cross the lines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible to do that. I watched, with my own eyes, how they expelled people from the new buildings in Radnicka Street, when they were telling these people on the Splitska and Belgrade streets, and then in the direction of the Vrbanja Bridge, and then towards the Energoinvest building, and there was firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was this not published in all the media, when this line was under the control and the monitoring of the world media?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know if it was published in the media or not, but I saw the expulsions with my very own eyes, people in columns with plastic bags and tote bags. After that, their property was looted down to the last needle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were lists for exchanges of population and for the joining or uniting of families organised by international organisations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: This was called the Exchange Bureau. It did exist. It was headed by some Captain Bulatovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, when we're talking about this column, I am stating here that after the army came and the lines were set up, it was not possible to cross over unless there was an agreement to do so and that nobody could expel anyone. And now I'm going to show a document. Do you know that there was -- there were lists? They come from the other side -- people come from the other side, asking that their families cross over to the Muslim side and the other way around; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: They did ask for each other through this Bureau for Exchange, and people were crossed over here and there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D2797, please. 1D2797. This is all in June, the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like us to be specific. If you did see a column moving, how do you know that this was not something that was done according to an agreement, and how can you claim that it was a line of people who were expelled, because there were lines at the time that were established and it was not possible to cross over without this being previously agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I could see from their expression that they were forcibly expelled. They were not going of their own free will. They were going by force. If a woman is crying, then she's made to go. She wouldn't be crying if she was going of her own free will and voluntarily. She wouldn't be leaving her property behind to be looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this was the criteria that you made this decision on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about other criteria?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The second criteria was if somebody was kicking somebody in the backside and hitting them with a rifle-butt, and cursing their Ustasha or balija mother, then I could see that somebody was expelling somebody from force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was kicking whom? Can you please tell us? If we need a closed session for that, can you please tell us, who kicked whom?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The Serbian soldiers were kicking civilians of Croat and Muslim ethnicities, civilian and military police and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I don't accept that at all. Can you look at this document, please? You can see here where it says that: "The UNPROFOR forces were rather surprised today when they came to the Serbian settlement of Grbavica in order to take several Muslim and Croatian families to be exchanged. These are families of Dervo Pusina, Izet Tanovic, Alija Talic, Drago Barbar, as well as family Hadzimesic signed the statement they didn't want to leave Grbavica because they had no reason for such action. To the team of UNPROFOR, they confirmed that, 'the Serbian authorities treated them correctly and that they enjoyed all the conditions for normal live, as well as the Serbian people in the settlement.'" They also asked how their names got on the exchange list in the first place. I am claiming now that after the lines were established, the only way to cross the line was if this was organised by some humanitarian organisation and what you saw was that. Are you able to provide some kind of convincing proof without reading the faces of people that you saw? Do you have proof that somebody was expelled, and can you explain how was somebody able to cross the lines who was expelled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Simply, they were able to cross the lines. They would tell the people who were at the lines to let them pass on the other side, and they were expelled, and that's that. Through Belgrade Street, you would be moving in the direction of Skenderija and Vrbanja, and that would be that. It was very simple, how this could be done. It can be done very easily if somebody wants to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you know about these lists?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know about the lists, but I know that through the Exchange Bureau, in some cases such exchanges were carried out, because prisoners were also exchanged through this bureau, and civilians were crossing either side. I know a Serb woman who crossed over to the Serbian side, she went to Belgrade, and then she asked to go back again, for example. There are different cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you say that agreement could be agreed with the line to let them go, the Serbs could reach agreement with the Serb line. But what about the Muslim line? Ten or fifteen metres away is the Muslim line.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Very simply, they see civilians moving there with bags in their hands, and they see that there are Muslims and Croats who were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The entire world would have known that, Witness. It would have been on TV. Such publicity would have been given that everyone in the world would have known about it. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: It's not true. It was on TV. You could see the bridge near the Bristol. If you remember the well-known football player from Zeljeznicar, Saracevic, how he was being expelled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? The witness knows that there was a commission for the exchange of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's a proper basis for us to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2798, please. We have the translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 23rd of June. The Sarajevo media said that a group of Sarajevo Jews from Grbavica were taken prisoner and that they were in the military barracks: "Blanca Romano, the leader of this delegation that visited the barracks, stated that the Jewish residents of Grbavica feel completely safe, having so far no problems whatsoever with the members of the Serbian BH Republic Army and therefore do not want to move from this neighbourhood." Have you heard of this kind of misinformation from the Muslim media?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I did not see anything like that, but it is true that the Serb Army did not treat the Jews in a hostile way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In a certain way, the witness has dealt with that issue of the Jews. Therefore, I think it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D886, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P998, could we have that briefly. It's already been admitted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, throughout the war there were three commanders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There was General Sipcic, and then General Galic, and then General Milosevic. I'm not going to refer to every one of the periods involved, but you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that General Galic was there and General Milosevic. I hadn't heard of that Sipcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. He was there until the beginning of August 1992. So please have a look at this document, which has already been admitted. We're not going to read all of it, but let us look at paragraph 4: "4. Provide for the safety of aircraft providing supplies to the civilian population in the area around the airport."

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't see that under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's in the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please. And in English, it was on the other page to begin with. So can we have the last page, not to read all of it, because it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, the last paragraph -- or, rather, the last sentence in paragraph 6: "Pay special attention to saving ammunition. Prisoners should be treated in accordance with the Geneva Convention ..." And so on and so forth. So it's the Sarajevo Brigade. That is in Novo Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: That is what is written there, but I have never seen this or felt this in practice. If that was the case, why didn't you say that on television, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Strictly Confidential."

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: "Strictly Confidential."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And all brigade commanders were issued this order. We are now dealing with the order of the military command to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It is strictly confidential. They are not giving any publicity to this. They are saying what they are supposed to abide by. Since this has been admitted, can we now move on to another document, P1000. You mentioned that the chain of command was operating. Was that the case, in your view?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I think that from certain points of view, yes, and others, no. As far as combat operations were concerned, I think that the chain of command did work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And violations were committed on their own bat?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: They were not even held accountable for violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at this document, and let us move on to the last page so that you can see what kind of orders are being issued by General Sipcic. He was a colonel at the time, actually. The last page, number 9. Number 9: "Have an impeccable organisation of the firing system co-ordinated with obstacles. Fire should be opened at military targets." Witness, you say that you did not see where shells were falling, those that were fired from Transit towards the city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I could not see their points of impact, but obviously they were falling on the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "should be opened," but it should be "must be opened." It should be in the imperative. Could the translation be revised, or could the transcript at least note the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, on Grbavica the Serb Army, or on the other side of the river, the Muslim Army, did they hold their mortars, guns, tanks on the front-line or somewhere in depth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: In depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If somebody is firing in depth and you cannot see the place where the shells are falling, can you infer that it is non-discriminatory fire, indiscriminate fire, or is it at a particular firing position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Our lines were so close that I can claim with a great deal of certainty that they could not fire at the line, but behind the lines, that is to say, where there was no military line. Our mortars, when they would shoot, often we received orders over the telephone that we should be in the shelter because the lines were so close that some shells could fall on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or there could be retaliation by the other side returning fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't think that our side could target the actual line with mortars, but they couldn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that there was firing in depth, since mortars and guns and tanks are in depth on both sides, in order to conclude that firing is indiscriminate, you would have to see the target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I could conclude, on the basis of where the barrel of the mortar was, where the shells were falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, then there would be no firing tables if you could conclude it on that basis, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I could see where the tank was firing. I could see that it wasn't the line that was targeted, but further in depth, where the civilian population was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a Howitzer and a battery of mortars by Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D576.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second commander, General Galic, this is the kind of orders that he is issuing to the 30th Division. This is just before he took over the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Just have a look at this: "Prevent looting, arson, private warfare in the area of responsibility of the division at all costs. Protect refugees and the innocent population, and the enemy should be treated in accordance with International Law on Prisoners of War. Those who violate these orders shall be subjected to the most strict legal and other measures, all the way up to physical liquidation." So these are explicit orders that are issued on the basis of International Law. Witness, the violations that you saw were not ordered from higher up, or were they tolerated from higher levels? Did you see looting carried out in an organised fashion anywhere?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: All of these individuals belonged to certain units. Why did Mr. Galic not check whether his order had been complied with, if he actually did order this, if this is correct? Did he check whether his orders were carried out, since he was commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is for the police to do. The police files a report, and then the report goes to the Military Prosecutor's Office, and then proceedings are initiated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Proceedings were never initiated. The looting went on. Perpetrators of looting and other crimes were never held accountable, they were never brought to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Because they were still there. They were not in prison, they were not anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you report any of these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I did not. I tried once to protect a Muslim civilian, as I mentioned in my statement. I went to the military police. I said what had happened. This military policeman just waved his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned shooting at the municipality. Do you remember that in the municipality, Budo Obradovic, president of the Executive Board, was killed, and by a Serb at that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I heard of the name, but I don't know who killed him or that he was killed, in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a court tried persons who killed others in 1992, for example, a Muslim and a Christian, because they were hiding in a cellar, and that the police reported that, and that the perpetrator was sentenced to 10 years in prison?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P1008, the first page. Here it is. So it is sent to all the brigades, to all commands. There is probably a translation, too. Yes. So have a look. The 6th of October, 1992. Can we have page 16 in Serbian and 11 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Special attention should be paid to people. Do not allow unnecessary sacrifices as the result of bad command, lack of discipline, sloppiness. Use all available means to prevent and punish those responsible for crime profiteering and indiscipline. Burning, rape, abuse, and inhumane treatment of the civilian population are strictly forbidden because that is incompatible with the morals of Serbian soldiers." So you do not know that such orders were issued and that trials took place, and that strict punishment was meted out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: As for the mistreatment of the civilian population, I'm not aware of anyone ever being prosecuted for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that people had to flee across the lines secretly if they wanted to reach Grbavica, people of all ethnic backgrounds, that they crossed over to our side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I heard of that, that such things did happen, but not while I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have 1D2773.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was work obligation and that there was military obligation, so military-aged people were subjected to military obligations, and work obligation pertained to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims, non-Serbs, had work obligation. Very few Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Serbs were trying to find ways and means of being transferred from military obligation to work obligation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that you said in your statement that Muslims and Croats did not feel right because they had not been mobilised, whereas Serbs believed that this was positive discrimination. Do you think that Muslims and Croats should have been mobilised forcibly or do you think it was better the way the Serbs had decided originally, not to mobilise Croats and Muslims, but to assign work obligation to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: At the time, people did not know what the nature of the authorities would be, you see. People didn't know what would happen, because in the JNA we were used to having units formed in such a way so that it would be people of various ethnic backgrounds there. So the question was: What would happen? Would it only be Serbs who would be mobilised or did mobilisation only pertain to Croats, Muslims, or whoever? As soon as mobilisation was carried out on a mono-ethnic principle, it could be seen, what this was all about. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in this case, a Muslim and a Croat could fight, if they so wished. There were entire units of Muslims who fought in Krajina, Posavina, et cetera. However, in such densely populated urban areas, the Serb side had given up on the mobilisation of Muslims and Croats, and they left it to their own free will. Would they be refused if they would report to a unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: This was not a matter of their own free will, whether they would do so or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a single Muslim or Croat who was refused if they were to report to a Serb unit in the Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know of any such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please cast a glance at this. December 1993, and this is what it says: "Sixty-one members of a Croat brigade crossed over to the Serb side. The entire shift by the Electro-Technical School crossed to the other side, and some went to join their families, and in this way went to Grbavica." Therefore, Captain Milicic, Djordje, informed that on this day in December 1993, 61 members of the Croatian brigade who were deployed across from Grbavica crossed over to the Serbian side. And that is something that you heard of as well; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed this, right, that this is something that you heard; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I wasn't in Grbavica at the time. That was the time-frame when I wasn't present, but I did hear of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That should be marked for identification only at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D2776.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the first sentence, it says here: "On the 19th of February, 1994, 14 people fled to Grbavica in the Serbian territory from the Muslim part of Sarajevo. They were interviewed. We have their statements, and we would like to report on the activities of Muslims at this point in time." Why don't you take a look at this document to see what went on on the Muslim side. And then in the footnote, it says: "Of the aforementioned number, 10 men got out, including one Croat, four women, and three married couples. Twelve persons were interviewed. One couple did not appear in the premises of this organ because Braco Lazarevic immediately took them away after they had crossed over." Was this something you also heard of, that this is how people crossed over the lines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know. As I have told you, I wasn't there during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This entire document speaks about the disposition of tanks, mortars, and so on, but I'm not going to delve into this because you weren't there at the time. We're not going to adopt this, are we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I see 65 ter 1031, and could I be given a bit more time, please. I'm not asking that we sit tomorrow, but could we have a bit more time today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is not minded to give any extension, given that you wasted time, but in particular, given that we have no other witnesses, that may possible depending upon the time necessary for the Prosecution for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, 15 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So I guess I got another 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You get 15 -- you conclude by quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at this order dated 22nd of April. There's still no Serbian Army there, just members of the Territorial Defence and authorities. It's an order of the Crisis Staff, and it gives the basis for the order and says: "All men fit for military service aged between 18 and 60, residing in the area of Novo Sarajevo municipality, are duty bound to report within 24 hours to mobilisation call (Assembly Point Lukavica - Local Commune). "They should bring with them their military booklets, all materiel and technical equipment temporarily requisitioned for the needs of the Main Staff of the Serbian Territorial Defence." And: "Whoever fails to respond to the mobilisation call and violates this order shall be subject to the Law on Military Obligation." And so on. So you see what this order is about. It's about mobilisation and requisitioning of trucks and so on.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't believe that this order was true, because there was absolutely no need for any civilian trucks and vehicles to be requisitioned because there was a sufficient number of the military ones. So I don't believe that this order was true or that it was ever implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know and do you accept that the JNA remained in Bosnia until the 20th of May and that this Territorial Defence could not issue orders to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that I saw military vehicles. I did not see civilian trucks being used. I saw military vehicles bringing in ammunition, food, and so on. Those were military vehicles, not civilian trucks, in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you that. Do you distinguish between Territorial Defence before the 20th of May, and that Territorial Defence had nothing to do with the JNA, it was not above the JNA or vice versa, it was subordinated to the JNA, and then the one later on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know to which extent the people from the Territorial Defence had influence over those in the JNA and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here only Serbs or all men fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Do you know what? The orders, themselves, were not badly formulated, but they were not implemented. Nobody ever checked to see whether orders were implemented, and nobody was punished for not implementing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us look at your case. On the 24th, you were supposed -- or, rather, on the 22nd, you were supposed to respond within 24 hours, that is to say, by the 23rd of April, and you did not respond, and nobody saw you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. This is the 22nd of April. The Army of Republika Srpska did not exist in Grbavica at that time. Such orders could not have been issued in Grbavica. They could have been issued in Lukavica, Vraca, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo included Grbavica as dominantly populated by Serbs, and Budo Obradovic was killed in Grbavica, at the headquarters of where he worked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, but it was later on, in May and afterwards, and this document refers to the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be adopted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do not really see that the witness adopted the document or the information, but I would not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we may need it in order to understand the witness's answer, in terms of context. It may be useful. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D888, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew Simo Sipcic. That's not the same person as General Sipcic. Another Sipcic; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke in positive terms about him, saying that he prevented some movement of civilians, that he sent them back home; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D2799, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was the head of military police in Novo Sarajevo municipality, a Serbian municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the document. I don't know if we have the translation. Yes, it is there. So the 22nd of July, municipality of Novo Sarajevo: "In the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the public law and order is gradually being established. "According to the statement of Captain Simo Sipcic, who is the chief of military police of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the civilians are respecting both military and civil authorities. All the difficulties that the citizens had are being effectively dealt with, regardless of their nationality. The number of citizens returning the illegally obtained property to the authorities is higher and higher. Because of that, the state -- the rule of law and order is being gradually but definitely reintroduced." Isn't that showing that authorities, themselves, in late July were not satisfied with the actual state of law and order and wanted the rule of law to be reintroduced?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: What is said here is a notorious lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They're quoting the words of Captain Simo Sipcic here. Are you trying to say that he lied?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I know because the civilian population kept -- was constantly mistreated and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, give us an example.

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you the example of the Balvanovic family residing in Grbavica. They were taken in the summer of 1992, taken away in early-morning hours, two brothers, their wives, and their mother. The five of them were taken away. The wives survived, and the three of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who did that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Veselin Blagojevic [as interpreted], nicknamed Batko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is about to be tried in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what do authorities have to do with Veselin Vlahovic, Batko? We are here discussing the position taken by authorities. There will always exist criminals, and what do authorities have to do with a man who was expelled and against whom serious measures were about to be taken when he fled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, they wanted to do it, but they never did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, did he just disappear from Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: While I was still there, yes, he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a basis to admit this, Mr. Karadzic. Although I allowed you a further 15 minutes, I would like you to be focused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Again, we see a document on how everyday life was normalised in Sarajevo, but I don't want to tender this so as not to waste time. Please tell me, when it comes to issues of leave and so on, do we need to be in private session? When I get to that, I will announce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said at one point in time that nobody ever told you what you needed to do once you were issued with weapons and given information about where you need to report, which positions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, no specific information was given, nothing overly specific. I was simply told that I should watch what's happening on the other side, that eventually somebody would appear, shoot, and so on. But we did not receive any strict orders as to how we needed to conduct ourselves and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned how somebody told you to shoot at everything that moved. Was that some sort of permanent guard or what was it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: We had orders to shoot at everything that moved on the other side. You can call it whatever you want. I'm not sure what the proper term for that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you ever on the line when an attack was organised precisely against the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The lines were never moved while I was there, and there was no attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ozrenska, Milinkladska Streets, the lines there went between homes; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers, when not on the duty, slept in one of those homes; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, in a way, those homes served as temporary barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Yes, sort of, where soldiers stayed when they were not on the positions and where they slept at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is how it was on the other side, across the lines; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: Well, how would I know when I didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the soldiers had to cook somewhere, had to eat somewhere, food was provided for them, and they could sleep somewhere when not on duty?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: We received food. We did not cook it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. In your view, if a unit of 10 to 20 soldiers sleeps in a house, would that make that house a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, I withdraw the question. If you surrendered your military booklet, was it entirely clear to those people there who -- that they had in front of them a soldier who had gone through a military training and who knew exactly what he could do and what not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No, it wasn't clear to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: They weren't paying attention to that. They simply gave us rifles, and had they been interested in that, they could have verified it. They could have put just three or four questions to see whether somebody was experienced or not, but they never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long did they keep your military booklet for?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: A couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you think that the Military Intelligence Service never conducted any checks to see about your background?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you shoot at everything that moved?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: I never saw soldiers on the opposite side, nor a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, please. You were on the ground floor, and occasional sniper shooters came to which floors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: The upper storeys of the building. They had better visibility of the opposite side from there. Now, which one, I'm not sure. They stayed on several floors, and on some floors they created fake halls, so I'm not sure exactly from which floors they shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see them kill somebody?

utterances.speaker: KDZ310
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we move to private session now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.
